extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, law students, and judges evaluating patentability (invention) issues
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and doctrinal rules for determining whether a claimed machine, manufacture, process, composition, or design constitutes invention (patentable subject matter), with case examples and exceptions. Focuses on combinations vs aggregations, duplication/omission/substitution of parts, new uses, and related tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination vs. aggregation (dividing line)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of this subject is well settled, and the dividing line between combinations and aggregations is well established. Every case must fall on one side or the other of that line, and no case can stand upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts of particular cases will often make it difficult to determine on which side of the line they belong; decisions may sometimes be made by direct analysis, other times by reasoning by analogy from precedents. Supreme Court decisions have tended to adopt the milder view in the cited language; pertinent cases are collected in the notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity of action not required for a valid combination
rubrics_metrics.description: "To make a valid claim for a combination, it is not necessary that the several elementary parts of the combination should act simultaneously. If those elementary parts are so arranged that the successive action of each contributes to produce some one practical result, which result, when attained, is the product of the simultaneous or successive action of all the elementary parts, viewed as one entire whole, a valid claim for thus combining those elementary parts may be made."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nor is it necessary that all parts of a machine combination co-operate all the time; "it is enough that, in the normal and progressive use of the machine, they do so some of the time." (cases cited in support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication of parts is not invention (unless new mode/result)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not invention to duplicate one or more of the parts of a machine or a manufacture; unless the duplication causes a new mode of operation, or produces a new unitary result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of non-invention: Dunbar v. Myers (additional plate performing substantially identical function) and Slawson v. Grand Street R.R. Co. (adding an additional pane of glass). Exceptions where duplication produced new operation/result: Parker water-wheel (two wheels face-to-face balanced forces produced new operation) and Goss duplex printing-press (stacking presses produced a new unitary result).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of parts is not invention (unless omission causes new mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not invention to omit one or more of the parts of a machine or manufacture, unless that omission causes a new mode of operation of the parts retained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission that merely reduces parts while retained parts perform same functions is not invention (Stow v. Chicago). Exception: reorganizing a machine so retained parts perform the work of omitted parts may be invention (cases including meat-mincing reorganization and process omitting a step after careful experimentation with increased utility). Mere making in one piece what was formerly two is not invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substituting an equivalent is not invention (unless new function/mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not invention to change a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, by substituting an equivalent for either of its parts; unless the new part, not only performs the function of the part for which it was substituted, but also performs another function, by another mode of operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a part is an 'equivalent' is further explained in the infringement chapter; the classification affects both validity and infringement: if the substituted part is an equivalent, the new contrivance may be an infringement and not an invention; if not an equivalent, it may be an invention and not an infringement. (Numerous illustrative cases cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining old devices without new mode of operation is not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not invention to combine old devices into a new machine or manufacture or design, without producing any new mode of operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule differs from the rule about simultaneous action because it depends on antiquity of mode of operation; invalidity under this rule requires outside evidence of prior art. Examples: Stimpson v. Woodman (substituting a prior figured hand roller into a machine was not invention), Heald v. Rice, Hall v. Macneale, and many other circuit and Supreme Court cases. Counter-rules: an old combination with a new mode of operation can be invention (Henry Adams corn sheller), and a new combination with a new mode of operation may be invention even if all parts are old; the statutory regime permits later superior combinations to be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using an old thing for a new analogous purpose is not invention (analogous vs non-analogous use)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not invention to use an old process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or design, for a new and analogous purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a new use is analogous or non-analogous is a question of fact depending on the particular circumstances; compare facts of cases where new uses were held analogous and where they were held non-analogous. A new use for a non-analogous purpose can be invention, and a new use that consists in combining the old thing with other things in a new organization may be inventive. (Many cases cited illustrating both sides.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Residual uncertainty resolved by Smith v. Dental Vulcanite test
rubrics_metrics.description: When none of the foregoing rules clearly applies and uncertainty about want of invention remains, that uncertainty may be removed by means of the rule in Smith v. The Dental Vulcanite Co.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text points to Smith v. Dental Vulcanite and a long list of subsequent cases as the test to apply when other rules do not settle the question; the referenced authorities exemplify application of that rule to resolve difficult inventiveness questions.
